stages.title: Colours
stages.hook: Look around the room. How many different colours can you find? Which one is your favourite?
explain: Colours are all around us. The sky is blue. Grass is green. A banana is yellow. Art uses colour to show how things look and how we feel.

Red, yellow and blue are called primary colours. Artists use them to make many other colours. Warm colours, like red and orange, feel like fire and sun. Cool colours, like blue and green, feel like water and leaves.
Artists everywhere love colour. People in Ghana weave bright kente cloth. People in India make colourful rangoli patterns on the floor for festivals.

example.q: What colour is the sun in a child's drawing? Think about the sun in the sky.
steps: Red, yellow and blue are the primary colours.
A sun is often drawn yellow.
Yellow is one of the primary colours.

analogies.home: Your crayon box is a little colour town. Every crayon has its own home.
analogies.nature: A rainbow has red, orange, yellow, green, blue and purple. Look for one after rain.
analogies.city: Traffic lights use red, yellow and green so everyone can see them.
analogies.farm: Green grass, red apples and yellow corn: the farm is full of colour.

stages.mnemonic: Red, yellow, blue: the three that start it all.
terms: What we see when light bounces off things, like red or blue.
Red, yellow and blue. They are the first colours for painting.
Colours like red, orange and yellow. They feel hot and bright.
Colours like blue and green. They feel calm and fresh.

misc.wrong: Only some people can make art with colour.
misc.right: Everyone can use colour. Children and grown-ups, in every country, make art with colour.

stages.limits: Some people see colours a little differently. That is normal, and art can still be enjoyed by everyone.

trip.prompt: Look at the rangoli pictures. Which colours do you see most?

questions.q: Which of these is a primary colour?
questions.why: Red, yellow and blue are the primary colours.

questions.q: Which colour feels warm?
questions.why: Red, orange and yellow are warm colours, like fire.

questions.q: Which colour feels cool, like water?
questions.why: Blue is a cool colour. It looks like water and sky.

questions.q: You want to paint a sunny day. Which colour is best for the sun?
questions.why: Yellow looks bright and warm, like the sun.

questions.q: You want to paint a calm, cool lake. Which colours fit best?
questions.why: Cool colours like blue and green feel calm and watery.

questions.q: Where do people make colourful rangoli patterns?
questions.why: Rangoli is floor art made in India for festivals.

questions.q: How many primary colours are there in red, yellow and blue?
questions.why: Red, yellow and blue make three.

questions.q: Match the thing to its usual colour.
questions.why: These are the colours we see most often on these things.

questions.q: A friend says: "I do not need colours to make art." Is that true?
o: No, art always needs lots of bright paint colours
Yes, you can make art with only pencil lines
questions.why: Art can be made with colour or without it. Pencil lines are art too.

questions.q: Why do artists pick warm or cool colours?
questions.why: Warm colours can feel happy and hot. Cool colours can feel calm.

panel.q: A picture shows a snowy night. Which colours show the cold best?
panel.why: Cool colours help us feel the cold.

panel.q: Why might an artist use bright red in a picture of a fire?
o: It looks like the real fire and feels hot
Red is the only colour left in the whole box
panel.why: Warm colours match fire and show heat.

panel.q: Choose one colour. Say how it makes you feel and why.
panel.model: Blue makes me feel calm because it is like the sea and the sky.
panel.why: Colours link to things we know and feelings we have, so there are many good answers.

teach.model: Colours are what we see on things, like red apples or blue sky. Red, yellow and blue are the first colours. Warm colours feel hot, like the sun. Cool colours feel calm, like water.

points.ask: Which colours do I need to start?

stages.title: Lines and shapes
stages.hook: Can you draw a house using only lines? What shapes do you need?
explain: A line is a mark made when a pencil moves. Lines can be straight, curved, zigzag or wavy. Thick lines look strong. Thin lines look soft.
Lines can join up to make shapes. A circle is round. A square has four equal sides. A triangle has three sides. A rectangle has four sides, two long and two short.
Artists use shapes to build pictures. A house can be a square with a triangle on top. People in every land draw with lines and shapes, from rock art to school books.

example.q: Draw a simple house. Which shapes do you use?
steps: A square makes the walls.
A triangle makes the roof.
A small rectangle makes the door.

analogies.home: Your window is a rectangle. Your plate is a circle.
analogies.city: Road signs use circles, triangles and squares.
analogies.nature: The sun looks like a circle. A mountain can look like a triangle.
analogies.sport: A football pitch is a big rectangle.

stages.mnemonic: Round is a circle, three is a triangle, four is a square.
terms: A mark made by moving a pencil or brush.
A flat form with an edge, like a circle or square.
A line that bends like a rainbow.
A shape with three sides and three corners.

misc.wrong: A square and a rectangle are exactly the same.
misc.right: A square has four equal sides. A rectangle has two long and two short sides.

trip.prompt: Look for circles, squares and triangles in the pictures.

questions.q: How many sides does a triangle have?
questions.why: Tri means three. A triangle has three sides.

questions.q: Which shape is perfectly round?
questions.why: A circle has no corners and is round.

questions.q: How many corners does a square have?
questions.why: A square has four corners.

questions.q: Which kind of line looks like a snake?
questions.why: A wavy line goes up and down.

questions.q: You are drawing a ball. Which shape do you start with?
questions.why: A ball is round, like a circle.

questions.q: Which line would you use to draw rain falling?
o: Wavy lines only, side to side
questions.why: Short straight lines going down look like raindrops.

questions.q: Match the shape to its sides.
questions.why: Each shape has its own number of sides.

questions.q: A kite is drawn with two triangles. How many triangles is that?
questions.why: The word two tells us there are two triangles.

questions.q: Why can a thick line look strong?
o: It makes a bold, heavy mark
It is always very, very short
questions.why: Thick lines are bold and stand out.

questions.q: A girl draws a sun with a circle and straight lines. What are the straight lines?
questions.why: Lines coming out of the circle look like sun rays.

panel.q: Why do artists often start a drawing with simple shapes?
o: Shapes are always finished art by themselves
Shapes make hard things easier to build
panel.why: Simple shapes give a base that you can add details to.

panel.q: Can a tall tree be drawn with a rectangle and a circle?
o: No, trees have no shapes at all in them
Yes, a rectangle trunk and a round top
panel.why: Trees can be shown with simple shapes.

panel.q: Pick something around you. Say which shapes make it.
panel.model: A door is a rectangle with a small circle for the handle.
panel.why: Everyday things can be seen as shapes.

teach.model: A line is a mark from a pencil. Lines can go straight or curved. When lines join, they make shapes like circles, squares and triangles. You can draw a house with a square and a triangle.

points.ask: Can you show me something to draw?

stages.title: Drawing basic objects
stages.hook: Pick a cup. Can you draw it so someone knows it is a cup?
explain: To draw an object, look at it first. Ask: what shapes can I see? A cup can be a tall oval at the top and a curved side with a handle.
Draw big shapes first. Add small parts after. Then rub out lines you do not need. Take your time and look at the object again and again.
Drawing is a skill, and practice makes it better. Artists in every country draw things they see: a pot in Nigeria, a bowl in China, a fruit in Brazil.

example.q: Draw an apple. What do you do first?
steps: Look at the apple.
Draw a round shape.
Add a stem on top and a leaf.
Colour it if you want.
example.a: Start with a round shape, then add details

analogies.home: Draw a spoon, a cup or a shoe from your home.
analogies.farm: Draw a hen or a bucket. Start with big shapes.
analogies.nature: A leaf can be an oval with a line down the middle.
analogies.tech: A phone is a rectangle with rounded corners.

stages.mnemonic: Look, shapes, big first, small last.
terms: A thing you can see and touch.
The line around the edge of a shape.
A small part, like a handle or a stem.

misc.wrong: You must draw perfectly the first time.
misc.right: Everyone starts with wobbly lines. You get better by looking and practising.

trip.prompt: Find drawings of simple objects. What shape do they start with?

questions.q: What should you do before drawing an object?
o: Throw it far away from you
questions.why: Looking closely helps you see the shapes.

questions.q: Which should you draw first?
questions.why: Big shapes first, details later.

questions.q: Which shape is best to start drawing an orange?
questions.why: An orange is round, like a circle.

questions.q: Which shape is best to start drawing a book?
questions.why: A book has four corners and straight sides.

questions.q: What is an outline?
questions.why: An outline shows the edge of an object.

questions.q: Put these drawing steps in order.
questions.why: Look first, build big, add small, then tidy.

questions.q: Your cup drawing looks wobbly. What is a good thing to say?
o: I can never be an artist
questions.why: Practice makes drawing better for everyone.

questions.q: A pot from Nigeria and a bowl from China look different. Can both be drawn?
o: No, only one of them can be drawn
Only if they are coloured in
Yes, by looking at their shapes
questions.why: Any object can be drawn by looking at its shapes.

questions.q: What is a detail on a mug?
questions.why: A detail is a small part.

questions.q: Why rub out lines you do not need?
o: To change what the object is
questions.why: Tidying makes the final picture clear.

panel.q: Two friends draw the same teapot. Their pictures differ. Why?
o: Each person sees and draws in their own way
One of them must be wrong, and one right, always
panel.why: Everyone draws in their own style, so pictures are different.

panel.q: Why does looking again and again help you draw?
o: It makes the pencil sharper and neater
You see more details each time
panel.why: More looking shows shapes and edges.

panel.q: Choose an object. Tell how you would begin drawing it.
panel.model: I would look at my shoe, then draw a long oval for the shape, and add the laces later.
panel.why: Starting with big shapes is a good method.

teach.model: First look at the object. Find the big shapes. Draw those first. Then add small parts like handles. Last, rub out extra lines.

stages.title: Colour mixing
stages.hook: What colour do you get if you mix yellow paint and blue paint? Try it and see.
explain: When we mix two paints we make a new colour. Yellow and blue make green. Red and yellow make orange. Blue and red make purple.
Green, orange and purple are called secondary colours. Mix a little at a time. Use more of one paint to change the new colour.
White paint makes a colour lighter. Black paint makes it darker. Artists everywhere have mixed colours for thousands of years, often from earth, plants and stones.

example.q: What do you get if you mix red and yellow?
steps: Pick red and yellow paint.
Put a little of each on a plate.
Mix with a brush.
Look at the new colour.

analogies.home: Mixing paint is like mixing juice. Two things make a new one.
analogies.nature: Yellow flowers and blue sky make green hills in a painting.
analogies.sea: Blue and yellow can make the green of seaweed.
analogies.farm: Mix red and yellow for an orange pumpkin.

stages.mnemonic: Blue and yellow: green is a fellow. Red and yellow: orange is mellow.
terms: A colour made by mixing two primary colours.
To stir two things so they become one.
A colour made lighter with white.
A colour made darker with black.

misc.wrong: Mixing all the colours always makes a bright colour.
misc.right: Mixing many paints usually makes a muddy brown or grey.

trip.prompt: Look at the colour wheel. Which colours sit next to each other?

questions.q: What do blue and yellow make?
questions.why: Blue and yellow paint mix to make green.

questions.q: What do red and yellow make?
questions.why: Red and yellow mix to make orange.

questions.q: What do red and blue make?
questions.why: Red and blue paint mix to make purple.

questions.q: What do you add to make a colour lighter?
questions.why: White makes colours lighter.

questions.q: What do you add to make a colour darker?
questions.why: Black makes colours darker.

questions.q: Match the mix to the colour.
questions.why: These are the three secondary colours.

questions.q: You want a green leaf. You have blue and yellow. What do you do?
questions.why: Mixing blue and yellow makes green.

questions.q: You want a pale pink. You have red and white. What do you do?
o: Add a little red to a lot of white
Add a lot of red to a little white
questions.why: Mostly white with a touch of red gives pale pink.

questions.q: How many secondary colours are made from red, yellow and blue?
questions.why: Orange, green and purple are three.

questions.q: You mixed too many paints and got a dull brown. Why?
o: The paint was too new and fresh
Many colours mixed together get muddy
questions.why: Too many colours cancel each other and look muddy.

panel.q: Your green is too dark. What can you do?
o: Add some black paint to it, slowly
Add a little yellow or white
panel.why: Yellow or white makes green lighter.

panel.q: Why is it good to mix a little at a time?
o: You can stop when the colour is right
It makes the paint dry quicker
It is a rule that all painters must follow
panel.why: Small steps stop you from going too far.

panel.q: Say how you would make a purple flower.
panel.model: I would mix red and blue paint together to make purple.
panel.why: Red and blue are the primary colours that make purple.

teach.model: When you mix two colours you make a new one. Blue and yellow make green. Red and yellow make orange. Red and blue make purple. White makes colours lighter and black makes them darker.

points.ask: What new colours can I make?
How can I change how light a colour is?

stages.title: Patterns and textures
stages.hook: Touch your jumper, a leaf and a stone. Do they feel the same? How could you draw how they feel?
explain: A pattern is a shape, line or colour that repeats again and again. Stripes, spots and zigzags are patterns.
Texture is how something feels or looks like it feels. A stone is rough. A feather is soft. A glass is smooth. Artists show texture with lines, dots and scratches.

Patterns are part of art all over the world. Ndebele women in South Africa paint bold geometric patterns on house walls. Adinkra cloth from Ghana is printed with repeating symbols. Many cultures weave patterned cloth.

example.q: Make a pattern with a red square, a blue circle, red square, blue circle. What comes next?
steps: Look at the order.
Red square, then blue circle, again and again.
After a blue circle comes a red square.

analogies.home: Tiles on a floor repeat. A blanket may have stripes.
analogies.nature: Zebra stripes and leopard spots are patterns.
analogies.music: A drum beat repeats, just like a pattern.

stages.mnemonic: Repeat, repeat, repeat: that is a pattern you can beat.
terms: A shape or colour that repeats.
How a surface feels or looks like it feels.
Bumpy, like a stone or tree bark.

misc.wrong: Texture is only something you touch.
misc.right: Artists can draw or paint texture so you can see it, even if you cannot touch it.

trip.prompt: Look at the bright shapes on the houses. Can you find a pattern that repeats?

questions.q: What is a pattern?
o: A single little dot on a page
questions.why: Patterns repeat in a clear order.

questions.q: Which one is a pattern?
o: Red, blue, green, then one more
Red, blue, red, blue, red, blue
questions.why: Red and blue repeat in order.

questions.q: Which feels rough?
questions.why: Bark is bumpy, so it is rough.

questions.q: Which feels soft?
questions.why: A feather is soft and light.

questions.q: Complete the pattern: circle, square, circle, square, circle, ... What comes next?
questions.why: The pattern alternates circle and square, so after circle comes square.

questions.q: How can you draw a rough stone?
o: With one smooth long line only
questions.why: Little marks make the stone look rough.

questions.q: Where do Ndebele women paint bold patterns?
questions.why: Ndebele house painting in South Africa is famous for its patterns.

questions.q: Match the thing to its feel.
questions.why: Each has its own texture.

questions.q: Stripes on a zebra repeat. What does that make them?
questions.why: Repeating marks make a pattern.

questions.q: A painter wants a fluffy lamb. Which marks help?
questions.why: Curly dabs look like soft wool.

panel.q: Why are patterns found in art all over the world?
o: Because a law says every artist must do it
People everywhere like order and repeats
panel.why: Repeating shapes are pleasing and easy to make in many cultures.

panel.q: A pattern is red, red, blue, red, red, blue. What comes next?
panel.why: The pattern is red, red, blue, again and again. After blue comes red.

panel.q: Tell how you would show a rough wall in a drawing.
panel.model: I would use lots of small dots and scratchy lines so the wall looks bumpy.
panel.why: Small marks suggest roughness.

teach.model: A pattern repeats again and again, like stripes. Texture is how something feels, like rough or soft. Artists can draw texture with little dots and lines.

stages.title: Light and shadow
stages.hook: Hold a toy in front of a lamp. Where does the dark shape go? What happens when you move the lamp?
explain: Light comes from a source like the sun or a lamp. When an object blocks the light, it makes a shadow on the other side.
Shadows can be long or short. In the morning and evening the sun is low and shadows are long. At midday the sun is high and shadows are short.
Artists use light and dark to make pictures look round and real. A ball with a dark side looks like a ball. Without the dark side it looks flat like a circle.

example.q: The lamp is on the left of a ball. Where is the shadow?
steps: Find where the light comes from.
The light goes to the right.
The ball blocks light on its right.
The shadow falls on the right.
example.a: On the right, away from the lamp

analogies.home: A lamp makes shadows on your wall. Try a hand shadow.
analogies.nature: Trees make cool shadows in the sun.
analogies.sport: At a football game, players have long shadows in the evening.
analogies.city: A tall building makes a big shadow.

stages.mnemonic: Light here, shadow there: the shadow is always on the far side.
terms: Where light comes from, like the sun.
A dark shape where light is blocked.
The brightest spot on an object.
Making parts of a drawing darker.

misc.wrong: Shadows are made by the dark.
misc.right: Shadows are made when an object blocks light.

stages.limits: In real life, shadows change as the sun moves. A drawing shows only one moment.

trip.prompt: Look at pictures with shadows. Which side do they fall on?

questions.q: What makes a shadow?
o: Too much sleep at night, in bed
questions.why: A shadow forms when light is blocked.

questions.q: The sun is on your right. Where is your shadow?
questions.why: The shadow falls away from the light.

questions.q: When are shadows longest?
o: At noon, when the sun is high
questions.why: The sun is low then, so shadows stretch out.

questions.q: Which is a light source?
questions.why: The sun gives out light.

questions.q: Where would you put shading on a ball lit from the top?
questions.why: The side facing away from the light is darker.

questions.q: What is the brightest spot on an object called?
questions.why: A highlight is where the light is strongest.

questions.q: Match the word to its meaning.
questions.why: These words help us talk about light.

questions.q: Why does a shaded ball look round?
o: It is painted a bright blue colour
The dark side makes it look 3D
questions.why: Shading gives the idea of a round body.

questions.q: Which object makes a bigger shadow near a lamp?
questions.why: Closer objects block more of the light, so shadows grow.

questions.q: A boy draws a shadow on the same side as the sun. Is that right?
o: Yes, shadows always fall on the sun's side
No, it should be on the far side
questions.why: Shadows fall away from the light.

panel.q: Why do artists add shadows to pictures?
o: To make things look solid and real
To use up all of the paint they have
panel.why: Shadows help show shape and where the light comes from.

panel.q: A stick in the sun makes a very short shadow. What time might it be?
panel.why: At midday the sun is high.

panel.q: Say how a lamp and a toy can make a shadow.
panel.model: The lamp gives light, and the toy blocks it, so a dark shape appears behind the toy.
panel.why: A shadow needs a light and something blocking it.

teach.model: Light comes from a source, like the sun. When an object blocks the light, a shadow falls on the other side. Artists use light and dark to make things look round.

points.ask: Which side does the shadow fall on?

stages.title: Simple painting
stages.hook: You have a brush, paint and paper. How would you paint a happy day?
explain: Painting means putting colour on paper with a brush, sponge or fingers. Use a big brush for big shapes. Use a thin brush for small parts.
Wet the brush, tap it on paint, and move it gently. Wash the brush when you change colour. Let the paint dry before you add more on top.

People have painted for thousands of years. Prehistoric people painted animals on cave walls. Aboriginal Australian artists, Chinese ink painters and Mexican muralists all use paint in their own ways.

example.q: How do you paint a blue sky and green grass?
steps: Paint the sky blue across the top.
Wash the brush.
Paint the grass green at the bottom.
Let it dry.
example.a: Blue at the top and green at the bottom

analogies.home: Cover the table before you paint. Wash your hands after.
analogies.nature: Paint what you see: flowers, trees, the sky.
analogies.farm: Paint a red barn with a flat brush.
analogies.city: A painted wall, called a mural, can brighten a street.

stages.mnemonic: Wet, dab, paint, wash: then you can paint some more.
terms: A tool with hairs for putting on paint.
A plate where you mix paint.
To clean the brush in water.
A big painting on a wall.

misc.wrong: Painting is messy and has no steps.
misc.right: Painting has easy steps. Cover the table, wet the brush, paint, wash and let it dry.

trip.prompt: Look at paintings from different places. What colours do the artists use?

questions.q: What tool do you use to put on paint?
questions.why: A brush carries paint to the paper.

questions.q: What is a palette used for?
questions.why: A palette is where you mix colours.

questions.q: Which brush is best for a tiny eye in a face?
questions.why: A thin brush gives small, careful marks.

questions.q: You change from yellow to blue. What should you do first?
questions.why: Washing keeps the blue clean.

questions.q: What is a mural?
o: A tiny drawing on a sheet of paper
A big painting on a wall
questions.why: Murals are painted on walls.

questions.q: Put painting steps in order.
questions.why: Prepare, paint, then clean.

questions.q: Why let paint dry before adding more on top?
o: Paint is shy and likes to hide
So the colours do not smudge
questions.why: Wet paint on wet paint mixes and smudges.

questions.q: Who painted on cave walls long ago?
questions.why: Cave paintings were made by people long ago.

questions.q: You want a wide sky. Which brush helps?
questions.why: A wide brush covers big areas fast.

questions.q: Can you paint with fingers or sponges?
questions.why: Painting tools can be varied.

panel.q: Why do painters keep a jar of water?
o: To drink when they are very thirsty
To wash the brush between colours
panel.why: Clean water keeps colours bright.

panel.q: Your painting got muddy because you painted over wet paint. How could you fix it next time?
panel.why: Dry paint lets new colours sit on top cleanly.

panel.q: Tell what you would paint for a happy day and which colours you would use.
panel.model: I would paint a bright yellow sun and green grass with red flowers.
panel.why: Many answers are fine. The idea is to choose colours that match the feeling.

teach.model: You paint with a brush and paint. Use a big brush for big parts and a small brush for little parts. Wash the brush when you change colour. Let the paint dry before you add more.

points.ask: What do I do between colours?

stages.title: Clay modelling
stages.hook: What can you make with a soft lump of clay and your hands? Roll it, pinch it, squash it.
explain: Clay is soft earth that you can shape. You can roll it into snakes, flatten it into slabs, and pinch it into pots.
To join two pieces, scratch both and add a little wet clay, called slip. Press them together. Smooth the surface with damp fingers.

Potters then dry the clay and bake it in a very hot oven called a kiln. Baked clay is hard and does not go soft again. People have made clay pots, figures and tiles in Africa, Asia, the Americas, Europe and Oceania for thousands of years. The Terracotta Army in China is made of baked clay.

example.q: How do you make a pinch pot?
steps: Roll a ball of clay.
Press your thumb into the middle.
Pinch and turn it to make the walls.
Smooth it and let it dry.
example.a: Press, pinch and turn the ball into a pot

analogies.home: Cups and bowls at home may be made of clay.
analogies.farm: Farmers once stored grain in clay jars.
analogies.nature: Clay comes from the ground near rivers.
analogies.city: Bricks and roof tiles are baked clay.

stages.mnemonic: Roll, pinch, scratch, join: now you have a clay shape of your own.
terms: Soft earth that can be shaped and baked hard.
A very hot oven for baking clay.
A pot made by pinching a ball of clay.

misc.right: Clay becomes hard when it is dried and baked in a kiln.

stages.limits: Clay must be used safely. A grown-up must always run the kiln.

trip.prompt: Look at the clay soldiers. What details can you see?

questions.q: What is clay?
o: A kind of thin paper sheet to use
Soft earth that can be shaped
questions.why: Clay is earth that becomes hard when baked.

questions.q: What is slip?
o: A slippery old shoe for walking
questions.why: Slip joins pieces of clay.

questions.q: What is a kiln?
o: A tall green tree in a park
A very hot oven for clay
questions.why: A kiln bakes clay until it is hard.

questions.q: You join two clay pieces. What should you do first?
o: Just press it hard once with a thumb
questions.why: Scratching and slip help the pieces stick together.

questions.q: Why should a grown-up run the kiln?
questions.why: A kiln is dangerous for children.

questions.q: Match the clay word to its use.
questions.why: These are simple clay skills.

questions.q: Where is the Terracotta Army?
questions.why: The Terracotta Army was found near Xi'an in China.

questions.q: Clay dried and baked in a kiln becomes...
questions.why: Baking makes clay hard.

questions.q: You want to make a long snake. How do you start?
o: Roll the clay between your hands
Cut it into bits with some scissors
questions.why: Rolling makes long coils.

questions.q: Which is made of baked clay?
questions.why: Roof tiles and bricks are baked clay.

panel.q: Why do cracks appear when joined clay is not scored and slipped?
o: The clay is too happy to stick
The pieces do not stick well
panel.why: Without scratching and slip, the join is weak and can crack.

panel.q: Why did people in many lands make clay pots?
o: Clay is rare, so each pot was valuable
Clay is easy to find and shape, and bakes hard
Clay pots never break, so they last forever
Clay floats on water, so it was used for boats
panel.why: Clay is common and useful for storing food and water.

panel.q: Tell how you would make a small bowl from clay.
panel.model: I would roll a ball, press my thumb in the middle, and pinch the sides up. Then I would smooth it.
panel.why: A pinch pot is a simple method.

teach.model: Clay is soft earth. You can roll it, pinch it and press it into shapes. To join pieces, scratch them and add slip. A kiln bakes clay so that it is hard.

stages.title: Creative expression
stages.hook: If you could make anything at all, what would it be? What would it say about you?
explain: Art can show what you think and feel. A painting can be happy, sad, calm or silly. You can make art about your family, a story or a dream.
There is no one right way to make art. You can draw, paint, sculpt, cut paper or use found things. What matters is that you try and enjoy it.

People everywhere use art to tell stories and share who they are. Bark paintings, masks, murals and quilts each carry meaning for the people who make them. We show respect when we ask about the meaning and listen.

example.q: A child wants to show a rainy day feeling. What could she do?
steps: Think of the feeling.
Choose colours, like blues and greys.
Draw drops and clouds.
Share what the picture means to her.
example.a: Use cool colours and rain shapes to show the mood

analogies.home: Make a card for someone you love.
analogies.music: Draw what a song makes you see.
analogies.nature: Make a picture from leaves and sticks.
analogies.sport: Paint the joy of a goal.

stages.mnemonic: Think, feel, make, share: my art shows I care.
terms: To show what you think or feel.
Events told in words or pictures.

misc.wrong: Art must look real to be good.
misc.right: Art can be real, silly, or made-up. What matters is the idea and the care.

trip.prompt: Find an artwork that tells a story. What do you think it says?

questions.q: What does it mean to express yourself in art?
o: To show what you think or feel
To copy what someone else made
questions.why: Art can show our thoughts and feelings.

questions.q: Which colours show a calm mood?
questions.why: Cool, soft colours feel calm.

questions.q: Is there only one right way to make art?
o: Yes, there is only one way
questions.why: Art can be made in many ways.

questions.q: What is imagination?
o: A kind of pencil case for school
questions.why: We use imagination to think of new things.

questions.q: Which can be used to make art?
o: Only gold and silver and jewels
questions.why: Artists use many materials.

questions.q: A friend shows you a strange picture. What is a kind thing to say?
questions.why: Asking shows respect and helps us learn.

questions.q: What is a mood in a picture?
questions.why: Mood is the feeling in a work.

questions.q: Put these in a good order for making art.
questions.why: Idea, materials, making, sharing.

questions.q: Match the art to what it might show.
questions.why: Different art forms do different things.

questions.q: Why do people make masks and paintings for festivals?
o: To hide from the hot sun outside
questions.why: Art carries stories and tradition.

panel.q: Two children paint the same tree. One is bright, one is dark. Who is right?
o: Both are, because they show different feelings
Only the bright one, because trees must be painted bright
Only the dark one, because trees look dark in real life
Neither, because a tree must be painted exactly as it looks
panel.why: Art shows personal ideas, so many answers are fine.

panel.q: Why is it good to ask what a picture means?
o: Pictures are boring until someone explains them
Everyone sees the same meaning in a picture
It is a test and there is only one right answer
Different people may mean different things
panel.why: Artists have their own reasons.

panel.q: Tell how you would make art about something you love.
panel.model: I would paint my dog with bright yellow and green so it shows I am happy with him.
panel.why: Art can show feelings with colour and shape.

teach.model: Art can show how you feel and what you think. You can draw, paint, make with clay, or use found things. There is no one right way. Share your art and listen to others.

points.ask: What do I do with my art?
